messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: negative variance with the "measurementInvariance" comand in lavaan - Where?
parts: a) Is it normal to have the same significance from the Chi Square difference model for all 3 models [MeasurementInvariance]? What is this caused by? How can i fixed it?

No, that would indicate the models fit the same number of parameters.  Your measurementInvariace() output shows that the models all have increasing df and chi-squared values, as more constraints are added on measurement parameters.  So I'm not sure what you think needs fixing.
b) Where is the reported negative variance? In my output I only see negative covariance for loyality~~experience. Is this the problematic part? How can I fix this?

No, covariances / correlations can be negative.  The model summary (fit3) you showed is a single-group model with regression paths between the latent factors.  So that is not any of the models fit in the measurementInvariance() function, which are multiple-group CFA models.

If you want to investigate the models fit by the measurementInvariance() function, you can save the output:

fits <- measurementInvariance(...)
fit.config <- fits[["fit.configural"]]
fit.metric <- fits[["fit.loadings"]]
fit.scalar <- fits[["fit.intercepts"]]

summary(fit.config) # no equality constraints across groups
summary(fit.metric) # constrained loadings
summary(fit.scalar) # constrained loadings and intercepts
Is it normal to have the same significance, 3 times? What is this caused by? How can i fixed it?

These aren't times, they are groups.  But you need to consider them in sequence.  The configural model fits well, but there is significantly worse fit after constraining loadings.  Until you resolve why, there is no point considering any further constraints (it makes no sense to constrain an intercept for an item when the loading cannot be constrained).  If you are unfamiliar with the concepts, I recommend not doing any more analysis until you understand what you are doing.  Roger Millsap wrote a great comprehensive book on the topic:

https://books.google.com/books/about/Statistical_Approaches_to_Measurement_In.html?id=7HisAgAAQBAJ&hl=en

To investigate why loading-invariance failed, you would need to test each item's constraint.  The partial() function (also in the semTools package, like measurementInvariance())  could be useful.
And the famous error message:

There are no error messages, only warnings.  The model converges, but it is warning you about a Heywood case, which may or may not indicate a problem.  Since you configural model fits well, the 95% CI for the negative variance might include positive values, indicating the Heywood case may mere by due to sampling variance. 

summary(fit, ci = TRUE)

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

parts: The chi-square difference was significant, but is sensitive to sample size.
Yes, that is called "power", and it always increases with sample size, given that the null hypothesis is false.  That is what you want a statistical test to do.
Therefore global fit statistics are considered.

chi-squared is a global fit statistic.  Are you referring to fit indices, which have unknown statistical distributions and therefore often have unpredictable sampling variability depending on the characteristics of the data and model?  There is little to no consensus an how to use those, despite how many applied researchers cite simulation studies that offer suggestions for cutoffs in the same breath as saying not to rely on those cutoffs because they may not generalize to other situations.
I conclude that the configural model obtains an overall a good fit, right?

CFI and TLI are high, indicating the model fits much better than the independence model, if you find that information useful in this particular situation.  Without seeing the RMSEA 90% CI, I can only say the point estimate looks good, although I don't really find "misfit per df" a useful criterion to evaluate model fit.

> fitMeasures(configural, selected)
   chisq       df    rmsea      cfi      tli

> fitMeasures(metric, selected)

But Milfont and Fischer (2010) write that at least one metric invariance must be established before continuing in the sequence of test.

You mean at least one factor loading must be invariant?  Well, you need at least 2 to be invariant in order to test whether they are invariant.  If there is only 1, you had simply better be lucky.  If you identify the model by fixing the first factor loading to 1, that loading is already fixed to equality across groups, but it is only the configural model (equivalent fit if you free all loadings and fix factor variances).  So you need at least one more constraint to establish metric invariance.

 https://doi.org/10.1086/209528
I have used the Modification Indices to identify which prarameters should be set free (have different loadings across groups).

The modificationIndices() function only returns indices for parameters that are fixed to a certain value (e.g., zero).  If you want indices to test equality constraints, use the lavTestScore() function.  You can compare the constraints in the output to those in the parTable() or summary() output to see how to adjust your syntax.
The global fit statistics fit well for the configural model with one free loading. But Chi-square statistic is significan, wich i claim is due to the large samle size (22626 obs).

Due to large sample size AND the null hypothesis of invariance being false, given your distributional assumptions are met.

CFI has 0 difference.

It has a .001 difference, but what does that mean?  Simulation studies have offered naïve cutoffs being valid based on average behavior, but Marsh et al. (2004) showed that their sampling variability is still affected by N, resulting in strange situations like power actually getting smaller as N increases (the opposite of what you want a statistic to do).  Chi-squared shows you clear evidence against the null hypothesis.  The question you are trying to answer is whether that difference is of any practical (not statistical) significance.  Differences in fit indices don't really help you answer that question.
Is this enough to establish partial metric invariance?

Partial metric invariance implies you can fit a model with at least 2 constrained loadings that does not fit significantly worse than the configural model.

If you want to evaluate whether the lack of invariance is of any practical significance, you could fit models with and without the equality constraints you find evidence against, and see the impact of those constraints on the difference between groups' estimated latent variances.  If the difference is approximately the same across models, then the measurement-parameter differences are not substantial enough to have an impact on inferences about latent parameters.

Terrence D. Jorgensen

parts: All improvements in chi-square are statistically significant - the null hypothesis that the loadings and intercepts are exactly equal in the population is rejected. Therefore the intercepts and probably the loading should not be contrained to be equal across countries...this also means that the latent mean differences for genders cannot be estimated.

Well, not all of them.  But as I said before, the differences in measurement might have very little impact on latent parameter estimates.  So don't lose hope, just compare results between a fully invariant model and the partial-invariance model you settle on (after testing individual constraints).
I have then applied lavTestScore() function and obtained results that i was not sure how to interpret:
I agree it is not easy to interpret the first time you see it.  Notice the total score test at the top?

total score test:

   test     X2 df p.value
1 score 60.201  5       0

That is the multi-parameter Lagrange multiplier ("modification index") estimating the likelihood ratio test statistic (chi-squared difference) if you freed all the constraints listed in the $uni (univariate) output.  Although it is possible to calculate the multi-parameter statistic, it does not necessarily correspond to a sensible test.  In this example, freeing all 5 of these constraints would result in a model that is not identified, so you should ignore this particular 5-df test.  

However, it is also important to note that the $epc output provides expected parameter changes on the condition that you free ALL of the constraints in the $uni output, so they do not correspond to the EPCs that you get in the output of modIndices().  I would not recommend setting epc = TRUE unless you are also using the add or release argument to specify particular constraints to test.  For example, there are 5 univariate (i.e., 1-parameter, 1-df) Lagrange multiplier tests, which correspond to the traditional "modification indices":

$uni

univariate score tests:

    lhs op    rhs     X2 df p.value
1  .p2. ==  .p95.  1.228  1   0.268

The integers on the left-hand side (row numbers) indicate that they are the 1st, 2nd, ...5th constraints listed in the parameter table.  The constraints themselves are indicates in the lhs, op, rhs columns.  So the first constraint is that parameter .p2. is equal to parameter .p95.  You can check the plabel column of the parTable() output to see which parameters these are, but they are also in the $epc output (.p2. is the v35 loading in group 1, .p95. is the same loading in group 2).  Thus, you can test each of these constraints, one at a time, by using the release argument:

score1 <- lavTestScore(object, release = 1, epc = TRUE)
score2 <- lavTestScore(object, release = 2, epc = TRUE)
...
score5 <- lavTestScore(object, release = 5, epc = TRUE)

Then you can print each test, and inspect the EPCs if that particular constraint were released.  Note that the uni- and total/multi-parameter tests are equivalent because you are only testing one constraint:

score1$test # total
score1$uni  # one parameter

You therefore get an estimated change of how any parameter (e.g., the latent fullfilment variance in each group) would change if that one constraint (e.g., the v35 loading) were freed, which can be much more informative than the only an EPC associated with the constrained parameter itself.  

score1$epc

Daniel Obserski has done some work on these, calling the EPC-interest:

https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpt014


Just a note on your model specification:  From your $epc output, it looks like your model syntax is not for a CFA, but rather loyalty is regressed on the other 2 common factors.  You need to test invariance using CFA (unrestricted covariances among common factors), not "full" SEM (i.e., no latent regressions).  Also, judging from the parameter labels, it doesn't look like all the freely estimated loadings are constrained across groups (e.g., fullfilment =~ v36 and experience =~ v37 are not constrained).  Is that intentional (e.g., using the group.partial argument)?
 
Saris et al (2009) suggests to us 0.1 as an "importnat" substantive difference in effect size estimate... Am i interpreting this right?

Unfortunately, lavTestScore() does not return standardized EPCs, so that criterion does not apply. In your summary(fit.loadings, standardized = TRUE) output, you can see how different the standardized and unstandardized estimates are.  Because you have ordinal indicators, perhaps there is very little difference, so the 0.1 criterion (or something close) might still be useful.
